newsitem.title: USA: ANR seeks FERC hearing on competing gas pipelines.
newsitem.headline: ANR seeks FERC hearing on competing gas pipelines.

text.p: In a bid to override a competing group's plan, Coastal Corp's ANR Pipeline Co asked U.S. regulators to weigh economic and environmental costs in reviewing two separate natural gas pipeline proposals in the Gulf of Mexico, an ANR spokesman said Thursday.

ANR Wednesday filed a request to the Federal Energy Regulatory Commission to hold a hearing on its $51 million Conch project, which would compete directly with the $220 million Nautilus project proposed by units of Shell Oil Co, Marathon Oil Co, and Leviathan Gas Pipeline Partners LP.
Both projects, proposed last year, were designed to handle new deepwater natural gas production in the Gulf of Mexico.
"We feel our project could accomplish the same thing as theirs (Nautilus) for a lot less money," said ANR spokesman Joe Martucci. "Ours would have less environmental impact."
ANR is seeking to add 461 million cubic feet per day of capacity to the 1.1 billion cubic feet per day of offshore Louisiana production it now delivers.

"Indeed, ANR can transport the entire volume of gas proposed to be transported by Nautilus, i.e. 600 MMcf/d, for a capital cost of approximately $51 million, by limited construction of new facilities and the maximum use of its existing offshore facilities," ANR said in its FERC filing.
"On the other hand, Nautilus must construct over $120 million of new pipeline facilities--which...will duplicate ANR's facilities--before one Mcf can be transported," it said.
Shell and Marathon have major deepwater acreage in the Green Canyon area to be served by the planned pipelines.
An FERC spokeswoman said the commission was unlikely to comment on ANR's request until it had decided how to respond.

In two recent cases in the Northeast and Midwest, the commission urged natural gas pipeline companies which had competing expansion plans to merge their projects in order to limit environmental damage and cut construction costs.
Shell and Marathon officials were not immediately available to comment.
